title: Networks including the internet
overview: This single subtopic covers the whole of the syllabus chapter on communication, so it is one of the broadest in Paper 1. You need to compare LANs and WANs, client-server and peer-to-peer models, topologies and transmission media; describe LAN hardware, Ethernet and CSMA/CD; explain how the internet is built from ISPs, routers, the telephone network and cell networks; explain the WWW, cloud computing and bit streaming; and explain IP addressing, URLs and DNS. Most marks come from precise definitions, ordered descriptions and choices justified for a scenario.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the purpose and benefits of networking devices, and the characteristics of a LAN and a WAN.
Explain the client-server and peer-to-peer models of networking, including thin and thick clients, and justify the use of a model for a given situation.
Show understanding of the bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies, how packets are transmitted in each, and justify the use of a topology.
Show understanding of the differences between and implications of wired and wireless networks, and of the different transmission media.
Describe the hardware used to support a LAN, and the role and function of a router.
Show understanding of Ethernet and how collisions are detected and avoided using CSMA/CD.
Show understanding of the differences between the World Wide Web and the internet, and describe the hardware that supports the internet.
Show understanding of cloud computing, including public and private clouds, and its benefits and drawbacks.
Show understanding of real-time and on-demand bit streaming and the importance of bit rate and broadband speed.
Explain the use of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, public and private addresses, static and dynamic addresses, and subnetting.
Explain how a URL is used to locate a resource on the WWW and the role of the Domain Name Service (DNS).

definitions.definition: A network connecting computers in a single room, building or site, owned by the organisation that uses it.
A network connecting computers or LANs on different sites, possibly thousands of kilometres apart, usually using links leased from a telecommunications company.
A network model in which servers provide applications, files or services that clients request and use.
A client that only sends input to, and receives output from, an application running on a server.
A client that carries out at least some of the processing itself, or downloads and runs the application locally.
A network model with no central server, in which each computer (peer) stores some of the files and can act as both client and server.
The configuration of a network, defining how the devices are connected by links.
A measure of the amount of data that can be transmitted per second.
A device that forwards packets between networks, choosing a route using the destination IP address; routers form the nodes of the internet.
A device at the centre of a star LAN that sends each message only to the device it is addressed to.
Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: the method used on a shared Ethernet medium to detect collisions and retransmit after a random delay.
The number of bits transmitted or processed per second.
A numerical address that identifies a device's network interface so that packets can be routed to it.
A hierarchical, distributed database held on domain name servers that translates domain names into IP addresses.
Providing computing services, such as storage, platforms and software, on remote servers accessed over the internet.

sections.title: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
content: Networking lets computers share resources and communicate. Connecting PCs in a LAN means software can be installed once on an application server, files can be stored centrally and shared on a file server, several users can share high-quality printers through a print server, staff can communicate by email, and files can be kept digitally rather than on paper. A LAN covers one room, building or site, is owned by the organisation, uses twisted pair cable or Wi-Fi, has user computers and servers connected to it, and includes a device that connects it to other networks. A WAN connects sites that may be thousands of kilometres apart. It is usually not owned by the organisation but leased from a telecommunications (PSTN) company as dedicated links, typically fibre-optic, with switches connecting each site. The internet is an internetwork: LANs connect to WANs, which connect to the internet.
bullets: LAN: small area, organisation-owned, high speed, end-systems attached directly.
WAN: large area, leased third-party links, connects sites rather than individual computers.
A benefit of networking should always be linked to a resource being shared or a task being centralised.

sections.title: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
content: In the client-server model, clients request and servers provide; on the internet the client is typically a web browser and the server is a web server. A thin client chooses an application to run on the server, sends it input data and receives the output. A thick client may do some processing before and after using the server, or may download the application and run it itself. Client-server is the choice when the server holds a database the clients access, provides a web application for finding or supplying information, or handles e-commerce and financial transactions. In a peer-to-peer network each peer stores some of the files and can act as a client (requesting a file) or a server (supplying one).
bullets: Peer-to-peer advantages for file sharing: avoids congestion at a single server when many users download at once, and parts of a file can be downloaded separately from several peers.
Client-server advantages: the organisation controls which files are available and who uses them, and files on one server can be regularly scanned and protected from malware.
Thin client: cheap devices and central management, but needs a constant connection. Thick client: can work offline and reduces server load, but needs more powerful hardware.

examples.label: Two-mark answer: roles of clients and servers
examples.content:
Question: Describe the roles of clients and servers on the internet. [2]
Mark-scoring answer:
Web pages and files are stored on servers. (1)
Clients send requests to the servers, which send back the requested pages or files. (1)

sections.title: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
content: A data communication system needs a sender, a receiver, a transmission medium, a message and a protocol. In a bus topology all end-systems share one link with a terminator at each end; every message is broadcast along the whole bus and each device checks whether it is the destination. It is cheap, but a break in the bus stops the whole network and collisions increase with traffic. In a star topology each end-system has its own link to a central device, normally a switch, which sends each message only to its destination; a failed link affects one device, but the central device is a single point of failure. In a mesh topology devices have direct links to several others, so messages can take alternative routes; it is very reliable but needs a lot of cabling. The internet's core is a partial mesh of routers. A hybrid network joins LANs that use different topologies.
bullets: Star is the most common LAN topology: easy to add devices and no shared-medium collisions with a switch.
A Wi-Fi LAN behaves like a star, with the wireless access point at the centre.
Justify a topology by linking it to the scenario: cost, reliability, number of devices and expected traffic.

sections.title: Transmission media: cable and wireless
content: Cable can be twisted pair or coaxial (both copper) or fibre-optic (light). Fibre is the most expensive but has by far the highest bandwidth, suffers least from interference and attenuation (loss of signal strength), and needs fewer repeaters, so it is used for long-distance and backbone links. Twisted pair is cheapest and is used for telephone lines and most LAN connections. Wireless transmission uses radio, microwave or infrared. Moving from radio to microwave to infrared, bandwidth increases but the ability to pass through walls decreases; infrared is limited to indoor use in one room, while microwave offers the best balance for most applications. Satellites extend communication to remote areas: geostationary (GEO) satellites at about 35,800 km appear fixed in the sky and three give global coverage, while medium- and low-Earth-orbit satellites provide GPS and support mobile networks. The long distances introduce a transmission delay.
bullets: Wired: faster, more reliable and more secure; costly to install and needs permission to lay cables across land.
Wireless: no cabling and supports mobile devices; more interference, limited range, easier to intercept, and some frequencies need a licence.
Repeaters are needed less often for wireless links.
For global links the competing technologies are undersea and underground fibre-optic cable and satellites.

examples.label: Delay through a geostationary satellite
examples.content:
Altitude ≈ 35,800 km; speed of light ≈ 300,000 km/s
Up to the satellite: 35,800 ÷ 300,000 ≈ 0.12 s
Up and back down: ≈ 0.24 s before any processing
This delay is noticeable in phone calls and games, which is why fibre is preferred where it is available.

sections.title: LAN hardware
content: Each end-system (a user computer or a server) needs a network interface card (NIC), which has a unique address set during manufacture that identifies the device on the network; a wireless NIC (WNIC) does the same job on Wi-Fi. A server provides a service, such as files, printing or applications, to end-systems. In a star network the central connecting device is normally a switch, which directs each message to a specific end-system. A repeater receives a weakened (attenuated) signal and sends it on at full strength, extending a cable. A bridge connects two segments of a LAN and stores the addresses of the devices on each side. A bus network needs a terminator at each end to stop signals reflecting back. In a Wi-Fi LAN (IEEE 802.11) the central device is a wireless access point (WAP), which connects wireless devices to the wired network.
bullets: NIC/WNIC: identifies the device on the network. Switch: sends a message only to the device it is addressed to.
Repeater: restores signal strength. Bridge: joins two LAN segments into one network.
A router connects the LAN to other networks such as the internet; a home 'router' often combines a router, switch, WAP and modem.

sections.title: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
content: Ethernet is the dominant LAN technology, standardised as IEEE 802.3, with generations from the original speed up to 100 gigabit. Legacy Ethernet used a bus, or a star with a hub, so every message was broadcast to all end-systems, each of which checked the destination address. Because the medium was shared, two devices transmitting at once caused a collision that corrupted both messages. CSMA/CD manages this: a device checks the medium for activity; if it is busy it waits a random time and checks again; if it is idle it transmits while continuing to monitor; if a collision is detected it stops, sends a jamming signal to warn all devices, waits a random time and tries again. Modern Ethernet is switched: each end-system has its own full-duplex link to the switch, which buffers messages until the link is free, so collisions cannot happen and CSMA/CD is no longer needed.
bullets: The random wait is the key point: a fixed wait would make both devices collide again.
Ethernet frames carry the source and destination addresses of the NICs.
Full-duplex means data can travel in both directions on a link at the same time.

examples.label: Four-mark answer: describe CSMA/CD
examples.content:
1. The device listens to (senses) the medium before transmitting.
2. Data are only sent when the medium is free.
3. While transmitting, the device checks for a collision; if one is detected it stops and sends a jamming signal.
4. It waits a random time before trying to transmit again.
(One mark per point, up to 4.)

sections.title: The internet's infrastructure
content: The internet was never designed as a whole; it evolved as networks joined together. Users connect through an access Internet Service Provider (ISP), which connects to regional ISPs, which connect to tier 1 (backbone) ISPs; ISPs connect to each other at Internet Exchange Points (IXPs). The busiest links are fibre-optic cables under the sea and across land, forming a mesh whose nodes are routers, each choosing the best route for the data passing through it. The public switched telephone network (PSTN) was built for voice. Early dial-up connections used a modem to convert the computer's digital signals to analogue for the telephone line, with another modem converting them back. Organisations could rent leased lines: dedicated, permanently connected links with a guaranteed speed. Today PSTN companies use digital fibre and act as ISPs themselves, offering broadband and Wi-Fi hotspots. Mobile devices connect through the cell phone network: the phone communicates with a cell tower, and the mobile company acts as the ISP.
bullets: Modem: converts between digital and analogue signals (modulator-demodulator).
Leased (dedicated) line: permanent, guaranteed speed and more secure, but expensive; used to build WANs.
Cell network: towers (base stations) give radio coverage in cells, connected to the wider network.

sections.title: The WWW and cloud computing
content: The internet is the internetwork: the physical infrastructure of connected networks. The World Wide Web is a distributed application that runs on the internet: a vast collection of websites whose pages contain hyperlinks giving immediate access to other pages, accessed with HTTP/HTTPS through a browser. Email and file transfer are other internet applications. Cloud computing provides computing services over the internet from large server farms. A public cloud is owned and managed by a cloud service provider and used by many customers. A private cloud is used only by one organisation: it may build and manage it on site itself, have a third party build and manage it on site, or have a third party provide it over the internet. Services can be infrastructure (storage and processing power), platforms (for developing and testing software) or software (applications run in the cloud).
bullets: Benefits: better performance and more storage than local systems, access from any device anywhere, no need to buy expensive hardware or software, and no need for in-house technical expertise.

Drawbacks: the provider can access all stored data, the user cannot be sure data are not shared with third parties, the user relies on the provider for security and backups, and access depends on the internet connection.
A one-mark definition: using services, files or software on a remote server accessed over the internet.

sections.title: Bit streaming
content: Streamed media are compressed and sent as a continuous bit stream that is played as it arrives, rather than downloaded first. On-demand streaming sends stored content, such as a film, when the user chooses; real-time (live) streaming sends content as it is produced, such as a sports match, usually via many content-provider servers because so many people watch at once. On the user's computer the incoming data go into a buffer, and the media player takes data from the buffer at exactly the bit rate the media need. Data should arrive faster than they are played so the buffer can absorb delays. The player monitors the buffer against a low-water mark (ask the server to send more) and a high-water mark (pause transmission so the buffer does not overflow).
bullets: The rate data can enter the buffer is limited by the connection's bandwidth, so broadband is essential for video.
If the buffer empties, playback stops to rebuffer.
Services offer each video at several compression levels so users with low bandwidth receive a lower bit rate at lower quality.

examples.label: Filling and draining a buffer
examples.content:
Data arrive at 2 Mbps; the video plays at 500 kbps. Low-water mark 100 KiB, high-water mark 700 KiB.
Net fill rate = 2,000,000 − 500,000 = 1,500,000 bits per second
Data to add = 600 KiB = 600 × 1024 × 8 = 4,915,200 bits
Time to fill = 4,915,200 ÷ 1,500,000 ≈ 3.3 s
With input paused, time to drain back to the low mark = 4,915,200 ÷ 500,000 ≈ 9.8 s

sections.title: IP addressing
content: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written in dotted decimal notation as four denary numbers from 0 to 255. It is hierarchical: a network part (netID) is used to route data to the right network, and a host part (hostID) identifies the device once there. The original scheme used fixed classes (A, B, C) with 8, 16 or 24 bits for the netID, which wasted addresses. Classless inter-domain routing (CIDR) adds a suffix giving the number of netID bits, e.g. /21, so the split can suit each organisation. Subnetting divides one network's hostID range into sub-networks, e.g. one per department, so addresses are not wasted and traffic stays local. Private addresses (10.x.x.x, 172.16–31.x.x and 192.168.x.x) are used inside organisations and can be reused by every private network; a NAT (network address translation) device lets them share one public address on the internet. A static IP address never changes, which suits servers; a dynamic address is allocated by the ISP each time a user connects, so addresses can be reused. IPv6 uses 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, giving a vastly larger address space.
bullets: IPv4 gives 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough, hence CIDR, NAT and IPv6.
In IPv6, leading zeros in a group can be dropped and one run of all-zero groups can be replaced by ::.
A router has one IP address for each network interface.

examples.label: Binary to dotted decimal, and CIDR
examples.content:
11000000 10101000 00000001 00001010 → 192.168.1.10
172.20.14.9/20 → 20 bits for the netID, 32 − 20 = 12 bits for the hostID
2^12 = 4096 host addresses on that network

examples.label: Subnetting one network for six departments
examples.content:
The organisation has one network: 200.15.7.0 to 200.15.7.255 (8 hostID bits).
Use 3 of the hostID bits as a subnet ID: 2^3 = 8 subnets, enough for 6 departments.
The remaining 5 bits give 2^5 = 32 addresses per subnet.
One network address is shared, instead of wasting a separate network for each department.

examples.label: Valid and invalid addresses
examples.content:
192.168.300.4 → invalid IPv4: 300 is greater than 255
2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 → valid IPv6
Shortened form: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329

sections.title: URLs and the Domain Name Service
content: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) gives the location of a resource on the web, for example https://www.example.com/notes/index.html: the protocol (https), the domain name (www.example.com) and the path to the resource (/notes/index.html). Routers work with IP addresses, so the domain name must be translated. The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server. If that server holds the entry, it returns the IP address; if not, it passes the request to other DNS servers in the hierarchy until the address is found. The IP address is returned to the browser, which then sends its request to the web server at that address.
bullets: Domain names are easier to remember than IP addresses.
DNS results are cached so repeat lookups are faster.
If a website moves to a server with a new IP address, only the DNS record changes, not the URL.

examples.label: What happens when a URL is entered
examples.content:
1. The user types the URL into the browser's address bar
2. The browser extracts the domain name and sends it to a DNS server
3. The DNS server looks up the IP address, asking other DNS servers if it does not hold it
4. The IP address is returned to the browser
5. The browser sends an HTTP(S) request to that IP address
6. The web server returns the page, which the browser displays

formulas.label: Streaming buffer
formulas.expression: time to fill = data to add (bits) ÷ (input bit rate − playback bit rate)

formulas.label: Transfer time
formulas.expression: time (s) = file size (bits) ÷ transfer rate (bits per second)

diagram.title: Looking up a web page
nodes: Browser asks DNS server for the domain's IP address
Browser sends HTTP(S) request via routers

analysisChains.title: Moving a company's files to a public cloud
steps: The company no longer needs to buy and maintain its own file servers
Storage can be increased instantly as the business grows
Staff can reach files from any device and location
But the provider can access the data and is relied on for its security, and access depends on the internet connection
analysisChains.evaluation: Public cloud storage suits a growing firm with reliable broadband; an organisation holding highly sensitive data may prefer a private cloud to keep control.

analysisChains.title: Replacing a bus with a switched star network
steps: Each computer gets its own full-duplex link to a switch
The switch sends each message only to its destination
Collisions no longer occur and one faulty cable affects only one device
But more cabling is needed and the switch becomes a single point of failure
analysisChains.evaluation: The extra cost is justified by far better reliability and performance; a spare switch reduces the single-point-of-failure risk.

analysisChains.title: Using NAT and private addresses in a school
steps: Every device in the school is given a private address such as 192.168.x.x
The NAT device shares one public IP address among all of them
The school needs only one public address, easing the shortage of IPv4 addresses
Devices cannot be reached directly from the internet, adding a layer of security
analysisChains.evaluation: NAT has kept IPv4 usable for decades, but the long-term solution to address shortage is IPv6.

examTips: Distinguish the internet (the network infrastructure) from the WWW (a distributed application of linked web pages) in one clear sentence each.
For CSMA/CD, give the steps in order: listen, send only when free, detect a collision, jam signal, random wait, retry.
For 'justify a topology or model' questions, link each point to the scenario (number of users, security, budget, reliability).
When describing an IPv4 address, say four groups of numbers from 0 to 255, 32 bits in total; for IPv6, eight groups of hexadecimal, 128 bits.
Explain DNS as a sequence of steps ending with the browser requesting the page from the web server's IP address.
Compare cable types using the same factors each time: cost, bandwidth, interference, attenuation and repeaters.
commonMistakes: Using 'internet' and 'World Wide Web' as if they mean the same thing.
Saying a switch broadcasts every message to all devices; that describes a hub or a bus.
Forgetting that the wait in CSMA/CD is random, or claiming CSMA/CD is still needed on switched Ethernet.
Writing an IPv4 address with a value above 255, or describing IPv6 as denary.
Saying DNS stores web pages; it only maps domain names to IP addresses.
Confusing a repeater (boosts a signal) with a bridge (joins two LAN segments).
Saying fibre-optic cable carries electrical signals; it carries light.

quickRecall.question: Give two characteristics of a typical WAN.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: connects sites far apart, not owned by the organisation, leased from a telecommunications company, uses fibre-optic links, no end-systems connected directly.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between a thin client and a thick client?
quickRecall.answer: A thin client only sends input and receives output from an application running on the server; a thick client does some or all of the processing itself.

quickRecall.question: Give one advantage of peer-to-peer file sharing over client-server.
quickRecall.answer: It avoids congestion at one server, as parts of a file can be downloaded from several peers at once.

quickRecall.question: Why is fibre-optic cable used for long-distance links?
quickRecall.answer: It has the highest bandwidth and suffers least from interference and attenuation, so fewer repeaters are needed.

quickRecall.question: What does a repeater do?
quickRecall.answer: It receives a weakened signal and transmits it again at full strength, so the cable can be extended.

quickRecall.question: Why is CSMA/CD not needed on switched Ethernet?
quickRecall.answer: Each device has its own full-duplex link to the switch, so collisions cannot occur.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between on-demand and real-time streaming?
quickRecall.answer: On-demand sends stored content when the user chooses; real-time sends content as it is being produced.

quickRecall.question: What does a NAT device do?
quickRecall.answer: It lets devices with private IP addresses share one public IP address when communicating over the internet.

quickRecall.question: Why is a static IP address used for a web server?
quickRecall.answer: So its address never changes and DNS records keep pointing to it.

quickRecall.question: What is the role of DNS?
quickRecall.answer: It translates a domain name into the IP address of the server hosting the resource.
